She wanted to try this one, since she loved the look of the design.
We figured how bad can a player be, right?
After seeing hers, my son ordered the same player.

Well, they do play music - for a while.
They also play videos nicely, albeit very small and hard to see.

As of today, with neither one a year old yet, one has had be to be sent back
to Sansa for work (totally locked up and could not even be rebooted). They took a
month to send back a refurb, rather than the one my son sent in with his music on it.

My daughter's lasted a little longer, but does freeze up often.
However, the latest trick is that it has part of the sound going out.
She had purchased four pairs of various headphones trying to get the sound to stop
cutting out, thinking it was the headphone's problem. Nope - turns out, it is the
player. Don't know what is wrong, but one of the stereo sides cuts in and out endlessly.

She'll be shopping for a new one, but it won't be this model anymore.
They are just too cheaply made to last. The technology has been around for a long time now,
and it shouldn't be that hard to make a decent, affordable player.
However, it seems like it might just be too hard for Sansa.

text_fidelity_a:
Creative Technology Speaker - Wireless - Bluetooth - USB, Bluetooth This is the second "Creative" brand wireless bluetooth speaker with microphone, and so far, the sound quality has not been very good. The first, "Creative Sound BlasterAxx SBX10 Wireless Bluetooth Speaker with Microphone" was $127.04 (list price $149.99), and this one currently has a list price of $199.99. I cannot hear any discernable difference in sound quality, though this speaker is larger than the other. They are both OK for being usb powered, but there are better-sounding products out there for the same price if you are willing to sacrifice the speaker option.

I ran the same tests on this speaker as the other and got identical results:

This one gets a mixed review for the overall sound quality, but it does have some features that make it very useful. I will be reviewing its various features individually so you can better assess if this meets your needs or not. I used a decibel measuring app on my phone to determine when the speakers began to distort some of what I played.

Playing audio with Bluetooth or via USB with a computer:
-There is no noticeable difference with playback using Bluetooth versus USB connection to a computer, and it has a Very long range (I walked about 25ft away and it was still doing fine)

AUDIO

75 DECIBELS AND UNDER:
Almost all audio was fine: clear, undistorted, and with pretty good clarity (don't expect GREAT quality or clarity. Just Good.) Some types of music fared poorly even at this relatively soft volume. I used "Fortuna from Carmina Burana" to test the system's limits. (YouTube the piece if you want to know which song I refer to--you'll recognize it immediately) The chorus of singers sounded distorted. At higher volumes, even as lot as 85db, it was awful. Other types of music were fine (orchestra music, pop, hip hop, electronica), but sometimes the treble was a bit fuzzy.

75-85 DECIBELS:
This is the maximum volume the speakers can reach with the USB connection, so it can get loud enough for a small-medium party, but not Very loud.
It's hit and miss here. The treble and bass have some problems, especially treble. The clarity diminishes and any nuances in your music will generally get a bit lost or muffled. Choral music, music with higher pitched percussive elements, and some types of rock and orchestra music don't sound very good.

PHONE CALLS:
The voice of the person you are calling sounds a bit muffled--definitely not as good as headphones or the phone, but about on par with other Bluetooth systems I've tried.

The voice of the speaker (i.e. You) is actually clear! This part gets a solid review. With my built-in car Bluetooth system, as well as detachable ones I've reviewed, usually the person you are calling has trouble hearing you and can experience interference. Maybe that is because it is in the car and there's road noise, but in any case, the fact this one does, actually, sound clear to the recipient of your phone call is a BIG plus.

Overall, this is a good product when you compare it to other desktop laptop speakers. If you are comparing it to products specifically meant for enjoying audio, however, I would recommend the Pioneer Electronics Audition Series for a relatively inexpensive but high quality experience, or Bose if you are looking for something higher-end. The price of the Pioneer product is almost the same, and while it doesn't have Bluetooth unless you buy the attachment separately (about $70) and it only docks with the older iPhone and iPods, the sound quality of that one is stunning. If you want extra features like FREE Bluetooth and speakerphone capability, this one is ok for the price. Not great. Just ok.

Because this is basically the same as the "Creative Sound BlasterAxx SBX10 Wireless Bluetooth Speaker with Microphone", and the other is about $70 cheaper, I would recommend getting the SBX10 and saving your money. They are basically the same thing, so either pay more and get better sound quality with another product entirely, or pay less for the same thing.
text_fidelity_b: Creative Technology Speaker - Wireless - Bluetooth - USB, Bluetooth

text_fidelity_a: TP-Link AC750 Wifi Range Extender | Up to 750Mbps | Dual Band WiFi Extender, Repeater, Wifi Signal Booster, Access Point| Easy Set-Up | Extends Wifi to Smart Home & Alexa Devices (RE200) I wanted this range extender so that I could stop using 2.4ghz because it has become too crowded in my neighborhood. The range extender only broadcasts 5G in the following conditions--straight out of the box when it isn't connected to the router, when you set up the extender to NOT connect to the 5G router signal, or when you select High Speed Option 1, which connects to the router by 2.4Ghz but broadcasts on 5G. So it's absolutely impossible to get it to connect to the router via 5G and broadcast 5G. I spent HOURS trying to set it up every which way. I repeatedly tried to set it up via WPS, via the internet, and after doing several factory restores. Every single time, the same poor effects. Having exhausted all possible ways of setting it up, I made the mistake of calling customer support. It was easily the worst customer service call I have ever experienced. I have lived and studied outside of the States and work with many, many colleagues who are from many different countries, and I rarely have trouble understanding someone who speaks competent English with an accent. However, the woman I spoke with was frequently unintelligible. I often had to ask her to repeat herself and could not answer her questions on the first try because it sounded like she was speaking gibberish. It was probably just the language difference, but she also had trouble understanding or remembering my responses, so I had to answer the same questions several times. Nonetheless, I reset the range extender with her over the phone several times. After forty-five minutes she told me that she'd have to have an engineer call me back tomorrow, at which point I said I'd just send it back and they can fix it on their own time. At one point she offered to email me updated firmware (the TP Link website only has firmware older than what came on range extender), but then at the end of the call when I reminded her of this, she said the firmware was universal and isn't even designed for this device. I asked her to send it to me. She asked me if I wanted her to send it to me. I said yes. She asked me again if I wanted her to send it to me. I again said yes. She asked AGAIN if I wanted her to send it to me, and I had enough and hung up. I hope this device is just defective as I've requested a replacement. If the second one works, I'll update my review accordingly. If not, I will promptly return it and be done with this fiasco.

text_fidelity_a:
idea display Q32P 32" IPS 4K UHD Gaming Monitor, 3840x2160, 60Hz OD4ms, 100% sRGB, 1xHDMI,1xDisplayport, 2xUSB,Type-C, USB-B, Remote Control, Frameless FreeSync HDR, LED Backlight I selected this monitor to work on a beefy laptop I use for building Linux virtual machines and testing software, so my use case is a little different than the target audience. I have been needing a larger monitor to go with said laptop and this one seemed to be a good one. So far I am pleased with it, though I have not pushed it to its full potential.

This is a 27" display capable of 2560x1440 resolution, fast refresh rates and bright colors. In the box comes the panel itself, a stand, and a DisplayPort cable. I was a little surprised that there was no HDMI cable in the box but this is all right, I have a couple of them so I was not left wanting.

My initial testing was disastrous, though the issue proved to be a fault with the laptop, not the monitor. My laptop has an HDMI output, and it does provide enough power to let the monitor know that something is there, but it intermittently sends a signal so I was not getting a consistent display. After a couple of hours, the monitor would display nothing at all. Thinking I had a dud, I connected a different system to verify and the monitor came right up. It did the same with a second system as well. After some research I determined that the issue was the graphics card in my main laptop which has known problems with HDMI. I bought an adapter to connect to the Thunderbolt port on the laptop and everything works fine now.

The system connected to this monitor is a gaming laptop that is running Linux with VMs installed. The system properly reports the model number of the display which is a very good sign. The OS does not push the monitor like a Windows gaming system might when used for actual gaming. For me, the screen real estate is what I needed. The adapter I bought caps the resolution at 1920x1200, so I am not getting the full resolution from this monitor but it is more than enough for my purposes.

The monitor responds to signal on both HDMI ports. So far I have not had occasion to try using the DisplayPorts on the back.

The display is very bright and clear, with no dead pixels. It seems to keep up very well with the system with no apparent lag, though again I am not pushing it as hard as I could. Because of the way I have it connected I can't bump up the refresh rate though it is happy at 60Hz. It doesn't appear to flicker to my eyes (though my camera disagrees), and it does not induce headaches.

If I could make any changes at all, I would change the design of the stand/base. The base is not height-adjustible so I cannot raise or lower the monitor without getting an arm harness. That's a minor complaint and is not enough to get myself upset about but it is worth mentioning.

Admittedly I am not the typical use case for a monitor like this, but I am happy with it nonetheless and it works well for me. The issues I have had with this monitor were related to other hardware, not the monitor itself. It seems to work very well, it is bright and clear and it gives me the screen real estate that I need. The fact that the Linux system recognizes its model number is a plus - it's supported.
text_fidelity_b: idea display Q32P 32" IPS 4K UHD Gaming Monitor, 3840x2160, 60Hz OD4ms, 100% sRGB, 1xHDMI,1xDisplayport, 2xUSB,Type-C, USB-B, Remote Control, Frameless FreeSync HDR, LED Backlight

text_fidelity_a:
JLab Rewind Wireless Retro Headphones | Bluetooth 4.2 | 12 Hours Playtime | Custom EQ3 Sound | Music Controls | Noise Isolation | with Microphone | Throwback 80s 90s Design | Black I wasn't expecting much given the price of this item, and I got pretty much what I expected.

The charging port is hard to reach and the LED charging indicator is difficult, if not impossible to see, without having to move the foam earpiece covering.

Setting up/pairing the device is pretty easy. Press the button for 4 seconds or so and you’ll hear a pleasant female voice say, “Hello”. This means the power is on. Continue holding the button and the device will enter pairing mode. You’ll hear the voice say, “Ready to pair.” When pairing is complete, you’ll hear the device say, “You’re connected” and tell you how much charge the battery has. So far, all I’ve heard is, “Battery full.” I have no idea what other battery indications the voice will give – perhaps only at 3/4, 1/2 and 1/4? Or maybe percentages?

The buttons are the biggest drawback with this device. Actually, it's really just one multi-function button on the right earpiece. The button functionality is not like any Bluetooth headset I've used before - very non-intuitive. The button has no label at all and the tactile feedback is nonexistent at times - I press the button sometimes and there's no "click" feeling. If a song is playing, it doesn't seem to matter where I press, the song stops if it is playing. When I press again, anywhere, it starts playing again.

There is no volume control on the headphones at all. You’ll have to adjust the volume from your phone/audio player. There is a bare bones EQ function. You control this by clicking the multi-function button 3 times in rapid succession. Each time you do this, the device advances to the next of 3 EQ setting – balanced, bass boost and JLab signature. The “balanced” setting seems to sound just like what it’s named – balanced or equal high, mid and low tones. The bass boos is decent – not overbearing. Not sure what the last one is, but if the pictograms in the manual are any indication, it boost the high and low ends. The EQ function does provide audible feedback – the voice announces each setting by name.

There's a next track function, but no function for going to the previous track. The next track function requires holding down the multi-function button for 2 seconds. There's no audible feedback for this function (other than a very short moment of silence). When you hear the silence, let go IMMEDIATELY. If you hold the button down for too long the Bluetooth connection will be severed and you'll have to reconnect.

Apparently, there's no ability to fast forward or rewind within a song or audio book. You'll have to do this on your phone/audio player. Pretty poor design if you ask me. BTW – I use this only with my audio player, so I did not test the phone/mic functions, but I’d be surprised if they were robust.

The instructions are minimal at best. The manual is one piece of paper printed on 2 sides. Unfolded, it's about the size of 2 business cards - about 4"x4.5" (10.16cm x 11.43cm). One side has instructions and the other is all promotions/disclaimers, etc. That's it.

Sound quality is acceptable - decent bass and stereo separation is good. I’m no audiophile though. The product description says it has "Noise Isolation", which is marketing speak used by all on-ear headphone manufacturers. It simply means the ambient noise is slightly reduced because the headphones cover your ears. Bottom line - there's no tech/function in this device that does any active noise cancellation.

The headphones are a little snug/tight, but not so much to be uncomfortable - at least that's my opinion after an hour+ of testing. Not sure if this will be true for something like a 3-4 hour flight. I’ll test this out in the near future and will update this review, if possible.

The charging cable that comes with the item is 9” long (22.86cm). Not very useful at all, but better than nothing.

On the plus side, the manufacturer did provide an extra set of foam earpiece covers - the set that comes on the headphones is orange. The extra set is black.

Bottom line, for $15 I wasn't expecting a lot - well maybe better button functionality, but hey, what can you do? As my granddad used to say, “You pays your money and you takes your chances.”
text_fidelity_b: JLab Rewind Wireless Retro Headphones | Bluetooth 4.2 | 12 Hours Playtime | Custom EQ3 Sound | Music Controls | Noise Isolation | with Microphone | Throwback 80s 90s Design | Black

4K HDR HDMI Switch, Koopman 5 Ports 4K 60Hz HDMI 2.0 Switcher Selector with IR Remote, Supports Ultra HD Dolby Vision, High Speed (Max to 18.5Gbps), HDR10, HDCP 2.2 & 3D (I have received this product mostly free in exchange for an honest review)
I have been using a 3-in to 1-out HDMI switch for a couple years and recently the media box for one of my TVs died, so put on connected to the single HDMI input. It works just fine, but I have more than 3 devices I'd like to connect and reaching to change the input is annoying.
This has solved multiple problems. having 5 HDMI inputs is a pretty sweet deal. I've only tested 3 of them so far and they work just fine. One nice feature that I didn't expect is that it doesn't appear to let you switch to an input that doesn't have a device even powered on, at least using the remote.
The picture quality is just fine. I have nothing to compare it to, but it looks no worse than it ever did.
The nice feature of my previous switch was that it did not need to be powered. The Koopman one DOES need power. It comes with the micro USB cable and power adapter, but if your TV has an open 5v usb output, that might be more convenient. I had to plug it in. It's a minor annoyance, but if you're low on outlet space, keep it in mind.
It's small and light, so I'll need to anchor it in place so it's not flying off the stand. HDMI cables like to pull things awry. It's almost inconspicuous.
Speaking of HDMI cables, it doesn't come with one. I had expected (and didn't pay attention to the product description - so MY bad) at least a short one.
The remote is tiny. This is great because it doesn't take up much space, but I KNOW I'm going to spend a bunch of events looking for it in the couch or under the footrest or because a spider dragged it into their web in the corner. The remote worked from at least 15-20 feet away (as far as I could comfortably go), BUT, the angle of reception is not very wide. It might be about 60 degrees (I did not pull out the protractor). The box itself had a button on it, so if the remote goes temporarily missing, you can still tap your way between inputs.
I'll give it some time to see how it lasts. If it does well over time, I'll possibly buy another for another TV with only one HDMI input.
One cool improvement would be if it had an audio output, even in only a 1/8" port.
text_fidelity_b: 4K HDR HDMI Switch, Koopman 5 Ports 4K 60Hz HDMI 2.0 Switcher Selector with IR Remote, Supports Ultra HD Dolby Vision, High Speed (Max to 18.5Gbps), HDR10, HDCP 2.2 & 3D

RCA Compact Outdoor or Attic Yagi TV Antenna – HD Antenna with Super Long 75 Mile Range – Long Range Digital OTA Antenna for Clear VHF & UHF Reception, NexGenTV ™ Compatible, Supports 4K/8K 1080p TVs The trick with this antenna is not getting frustrated with moving it around and pointing it in the right direction. I mounted mine on the hand rail of my apartment balcony, second floor and now receive all local channels 4-68. Channel 68 being about 45 miles away. All are received in full green in windows media center, without using a preamp.

Previously I had it mounted under and bolted to the 3rd floor balcony to try and keep it out of sight. Reception was iffy on 4 favorite channels. I then moved it to its' present location with the idea that the antennas footprint is considerably smaller than all the satellite dishes mounted on balconies throughout the complex. The mounting bracket and pole that come with it, are the same type satellite dishes use, Very strong and versatile. You will need to buy some good bolts, I used 4, 5/16" x 1- 1/2" Galvanized Lag and flat washers, I predrilled 3/16" pilot holes first. I just thought I'd mention that for those not fastener savvy.

I would guess the antenna mount alone is worth 1/3rd of the entire antenna cost. Recommend a good quad shield coaxial cable with the thick, sollid copper wire. A shorter run is better if possible. I only have about 12 feet to my PC/TV.

Once I figured out how to mount this antenna correctly, a month ago, I haven't had to adjust it.

text_fidelity_a:
FULLJA WiFi Digital Picture Frame - 10.1 Inch Smart Digital Photo Frame with FHD IPS Touch Screen, 32GB Memory, Motion Sensor WiFi Electronic Picture Frame Share Photos and Videos Via App Email I don’t love it. This seems overpriced for what you get. For the price, I was expecting it to look more like a photo frame but instead, it kinda feels like an old monitor. My goal was to hang it on the wall during art shows with process videos playing. It will work OK for that but I’m disappointed that unless the video is in the exact proportion of the frame, it will always look a little “off” and there’s no means of changing how it’s framed in the display.

I think it’s at its best without the clock or any other additions.

The pros: It really does work right out of the box. It only took minutes to get photos onto it. The big screen is nice, I can see details in my photos. It is also bright with vivid colors. I like that it is flat which is why it performs better than an average monitor as a picture frame. The simple black frame doesn’t detract from its appearance. I like that there is an app and my husband and I were able to add photos, and I also like that there is a way to add photos via card in case software changes make the app obsolete. With the app, I was able to get videos onto it in minutes. I also like that it has a large amount of storage space and the means to expand it..

The cons: It is slow. I didn’t love the way the photos are displayed. I also hate the default animations because they are a bit cheesy. I want it to fade or some other non-intrusive way to change photos, and there is no means to edit it. The features are incredibly barebones. I hate that the default includes the time etc, I just want it to look like a photo frame! The audio is a bit tinny, much more so than a television etc. I also find it bizarre in 2023 to have an item that warns that it can destroy a USB if it’s removed without turning it off first…that seems like such an old-school problem!

I wish the plug was white because the black looks bad against the wall, and I prefer a minimalist look.

For the price, I feel like this could be better. There are just so few options for customizing the display.
text_fidelity_b: FULLJA WiFi Digital Picture Frame - 10.1 Inch Smart Digital Photo Frame with FHD IPS Touch Screen, 32GB Memory, Motion Sensor WiFi Electronic Picture Frame Share Photos and Videos Via App Email
